ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, Figure A and Figure B respectively represent the changing relationship between alternating current and time for a sinusoidal pulse wave and a square wave. If these two kinds of currents are respectively made to pass through two completely identical resistors, then after a time of 1 min, what is the ratio of the electric work consumed by the two resistors W_A∶W_B?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the upper Figure A is a sinusoidal pulse wave in which current i changes with time t; the vertical axis marks peak values of about +1 A and -1 A, and the horizontal-axis unit is ×10^-2 s. In Figure A, the positive and negative half-sinusoidal pulses each last about 2×10^-2 s, and between adjacent pulses there is a segment of about 2×10^-2 s during which the current is 0; judging from the repetition of the graph, one period is 6×10^-2 s. The lower Figure B is a square wave, and the current changes only between +1 A and -1 A, always satisfying |i|=1 A. Then reason: the electric work consumed by identical resistors in the same time is W=∫i^2Rdt, so the ratio of W is equal to the ratio of ∫i^2dt, and is also equal to the ratio of the mean square currents. Within one period of Figure A, the two half-sinusoidal pulses each last 2×10^-2 s, and the average value of i^2 for half of a sinusoidal pulse is half of the square of the peak value, namely 1^2/2, so ∫i^2dt=2×(2×10^-2)×(1/2)=2×10^-2 A^2·s. The period of Figure A is 6×10^-2 s, so the average i^2 is (2×10^-2)/(6×10^-2)=1/3 A^2. Figure B always has |i|=1 A, so the average i^2=1 A^2. For both kinds of periodic waves, 1 min is a complete large number of periods, so the ratio of electric work is W_A:W_B=(1/3):1=1:3.
